title: How an LED works
body: LED stands for light-emitting diode. A diode lets current through in one direction only: in at the anode (the longer leg) and out at the cathode. Put it in backwards and it won't light.
A red LED needs about 2 volts across it before much current flows. It's designed for a small current, typically 10 to 20 milliamps, with a maximum of about 30 mA.

Above about 2 V, the current climbs steeply with every extra bit of voltage. Connect an LED straight to a battery and the current shoots past its limit until it burns out. A resistor in series holds the current at a safe level.
realWorld: LED lamps, phone screens and bike lights all include a resistor or a driver chip that keeps the LEDs' current in check.
sources: OpenStax University Physics Volume 3, §9.7 Semiconductor Devices. https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-3/pages/9-7-semiconductor-devices
